dct_description_sm: The late-stage tectonometamorphic evolution of the Paleoproterozoic Ungava orogen (UO), a segment of the Trans-Hudson orogen, remains poorly understood due to limited structural and geochronological data. This study presents new, integrated field-based mapping, microstructural characterization, thermometry, apatite and biotite trace element analysis, and in situ U-Pb and Rb-Sr geochronology to investigate the late-stage evolution of the Narsajuaq domain of the UO. Examination of internal structural domain boundaries reveals distributed strain zones with opposing transport directions across adjacent boundaries, consistent with a complex structural history, including a newly recognized E–W-striking lateral ramp. Mineral assemblages and thermometry data indicate that deformation continued during post-peak amphibolite-facies retrogression. Geochronological data outline five broad groups spanning multiple mineral chronometers, including an early Paleoproterozoic component, a metamorphic and/or magmatic high-temperature event at ca. 1865 Ma, a principal post-peak population with modes at ca. 1750–1740 Ma and 1710–1705 Ma, and a late ca. 1545 Ma component. The older mode may, in part, reflect fluid-assisted isotopic resetting, whereas the younger mode is compatible with regional cooling. The spatial coincidence of structural domain boundaries with distributed strain provides a potential framework for fluid circulation and associated late-stage isotopic modification during retrogression and cooling. These results demonstrate that the Narsajuaq domain preserves tectonothermal activity beyond the commonly cited ca. 1.80 Ga end of Trans-Hudson orogenesis. More broadly, this study highlights the value of integrating structural observations, microstructural analysis, thermometry, and petrochronology in resolving late- to post-orogenic processes that may not be evident from any single dataset alone.
